collection.label: Sanchuniathon, Phoenician History
collection.author_name: Philo of Byblos (c. 100 AD), translating Sanchuniathon, in Eusebius
collection.critical_edition: W. Dindorf, Eusebii Caesariensis opera I (Teubner 1867), First1KGreek, proofread
collection.search_terms: sanchuniathon sanchoniathon philo byblos phoenician history eusebius praeparatio evangelica kronos elus uranus taautus thoth astarte dagon byblos tyre
collection.description: The Phoenician account of the beginning of the world, the first inventors, and the reigns of Uranus, Kronos (El) and Astarte, from Philo of Byblos' Greek translation of Sanchuniathon, on the pages of the Arethas codex of Eusebius written in 914 AD.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon and Philo of Byblos: Porphyry's testimony and Philo's preface (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.9.20-30)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Eusebius introduces Sanchuniathon of Berytus, older than the Trojan War, whose Phoenician History Philo of Byblos translated into Greek; Porphyry's testimony that he drew on the records of the priest Hierombalus; and Philo's preface on Taautus, inventor of writing, and on the later priests who turned history into allegory.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: the Phoenician cosmogony and the first worship (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.1-8)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: The beginning of all things in Philo's translation of Sanchuniathon: dark air and chaos, the wind's desire, Mot and the egg-shaped Zophasemin, the 'observers of heaven', thunder waking the first living things, and the first men who worshipped the plants of the earth and the sun as Beelsamen, lord of heaven.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: the first generations and the inventors of the arts (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.9-14)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: The generations after Aeon and Protogonus: Light, Fire and Flame who discovered fire, the giants who gave their names to Lebanon and Mount Cassius, Hypsuranius who built huts at Tyre and Ousoos who first went to sea, Chrysor who invented iron-working and sailing, the builders of brick, the shepherds, Misor and Sydyk who found salt, and Taautus who invented writing.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: Uranus, Ge and the reign of Kronos (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.15-30)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Uranus and Ge, the war of their son Elus or Kronos against his father, the founding of Byblos as the first city, the baetyls or living stones, the children of Kronos and Astarte, Dagon who found grain and the plough, and the mutilation of Uranus near springs and rivers.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: Astarte, the deeds of Kronos and the symbols of Taautus (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.31-41)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Astarte with the head of a bull and the star she found and dedicated at Tyre, Kronos' sacrifice of his only son and his gifts of cities, the four eyes and six wings Taautus devised as the insignia of Kronos, the gift of Egypt to Taautus, the records kept by the Cabeiri, and Philo's complaint that the Greeks turned these stories into myth.

texts.title: Philo of Byblos on Taautus, royal sacrifice and the serpent, with Eusebius' conclusion (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.42-55)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Further passages of Philo: Taautus who first set religion in order, the ancient custom of sacrificing a ruler's beloved son in times of danger, and the serpent, which Taautus held divine, the good daemon of the Phoenicians and the Egyptian Kneph, followed by Eusebius' closing words on the Phoenician theology.

authors.name: Philo of Byblos
authors.bio: Phoenician grammarian and historian from Byblos who wrote in Greek; his Phoenician History, presented as a translation of the ancient writer Sanchuniathon, survives in quotations by Eusebius.
